Hugh Everett III is a mathematician. Hugh Everett III (November 11, 1930 – July 19, 1982) was an American physicist who proposed the relative state interpretation of quantum mechanics.
What is the atomic number of Tin?
Tin is a chemical element; it has the symbol Sn (from Latin stannum) and atomic number 50.
What is the atomic number of Titanium?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
In what year was Archimedes born?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year was Huntington's disease discovered?
Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.
Swift (programming language): Apple Inc. Swift compiles to machine code and uses an LLVM-based compiler.
Levofloxacin: Pfizer. Levofloxacin, sold under the brand name Levaquin among others, is a broad-spectrum antibiotic of the fluoroquinolone drug class.
In which country is Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker?
Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker: United States. It has a narrower fuselage and is shorter than the 707.
Who is credited with discovering Roentgenium?
GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
Roentgenium: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. Roentgenium (German: [ʁœntˈɡeːni̯ʊm]) is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
Who is credited with discovering 4 Vesta?
4 Vesta: Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers. Vesta (minor-planet designation: 4 Vesta) is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt, with a mean diameter of 525 kilometres (326 mi).
Who is credited with discovering Lysosome?
Lysosome: Christian de Duve. A lysosome (/ˈlaɪsəˌsoʊm/) is a membrane-bound organelle that is found in all animal cells (except red blood cells), and rarely in plant cells.
Sometimes called ajowan caraway or carom, this annual herb in the carrot family produces a seed-like fruit often confused with lovage — what is it?
Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) - also known as ajowan caraway, thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom - is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.
Despite overseeing Soviet thermonuclear weapons development, this physicist won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize for his activism on human rights and individual freedom — who is he?
Andrei Sakharov (21 May 1921 - 14 December 1989) was a Soviet physicist and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, which he was awarded in 1975 for emphasizing human rights around the world.
Named from the Ancient Greek word for silver, this condition results from too much silver exposure and can leave the skin permanently blue-gray — what is it?
Argyria is a condition caused by excessive exposure to chemical compounds of the element silver, or silver dust.
This large bird of prey is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists mostly — 70 to 90 percent — of bone. What bird is it?
Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), also known as the lammergeier and ossifrage, is a very large bird of prey in the monotypic genus Gypaetus.
Around 2,500 species of this insect family defend themselves by secreting a skin-irritating toxin called cantharidin, often flaunting bold warning colors — which family?
Blister beetle are beetles of the family Meloidae, so called for their defensive secretion of a blistering agent, cantharidin.
The only living group in its tribe, this genus of over 250 fuzzy bees forms small colonies under a single queen — and unlike honeybees, its females can sting again and again — what is it?
Bumblebee (or bumble bee, bumble-bee, or humble-bee) is any of over 250 species in the genus Bombus, part of Apidae, one of the bee families.
This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' and studies cell-surface sugars called glycans from her professorship at Stanford — who is she?
Carolyn Bertozzi (born October 10, 1966) is an American chemist and Nobel laureate, known for her wide-ranging work spanning both chemistry and biology.
Defined by a hollow dorsal nerve cord, an endostyle, and a post-anal tail at some point in life, this phylum spans vertebrates, tunicates, and lancelets alike — which option fits?
Chordate is a bilaterian animal belonging to the phylum Chordata (kor-).
Though it resembles a barn swallow, this medium-sized bird is actually more closely related to hummingbirds than to any swallow, its resemblance being pure convergent evolution — what bird is it?

Common swift (Apus apus) is a medium-sized bird, superficially similar to the barn swallow or house martin but somewhat larger, though not stemming from those passerine species, being in the order Apodiformes.
Present in the cytoplasm of bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotic cells alike, this dynamic protein-filament network stabilizes tissue and enables cells to migrate — what is it?
Cytoskeleton is a complex, dynamic network of interlinking protein filaments present in the cytoplasm of all cells, including those of bacteria and archaea.
This Canadian optical physicist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing chirped pulse amplification, a breakthrough in pulsed lasers. Who is she?
Donna Strickland (born May 27, 1959) is a Canadian optical physicist and pioneer in the field of pulsed lasers.
What medical condition, caused by viruses like herpes simplex or rabies, bacteria, or autoimmune disease, refers to inflammation of the brain and can cause confusion, seizures, and memory problems?

Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain. The severity can be variable with symptoms including reduction or alteration in consciousness, aphasia, headache, fever, confusion, a stiff neck, and vomiting.
Known for filling pillows and blankets as well as lining the wings of birds, what are these soft, complex integumentary structures called?
Feather are epidermal growths that form a distinctive outer covering, or plumage, on both avian (bird) and some non-avian dinosaurs and other archosaurs.
Co-author of 'The Communist Manifesto' and lifelong collaborator with Karl Marx, this German theorist finished the second and third volumes of 'Das Kapital' after his partner's death — who is he?
Friedrich Engels (28 November 1820 - 5 August 1895) was a German philosopher, social and political theorist, journalist, businessman, and revolutionary socialist.
A group 11 noble metal that forms a natural alloy called electrum with silver, this element takes its symbol from the Latin aurum — what is it?
Gold is a chemical element; its chemical symbol is Au (from Latin aurum) and atomic number 79.
Confirming Maxwell's theoretical predictions, this 19th-century German physicist proved that electromagnetic waves actually exist — who is he?

Heinrich Hertz (hurts; 22 February 1857 - 1 January 1894) was a German physicist who first conclusively proved the existence of the electromagnetic waves proposed by James Clerk Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism.
This semi-synthetic opioid, often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, treats severe pain and also suppresses cough — what drug is it?
Hydrocodone is a semi-synthetic opioid used to treat pain and as a cough suppressant.
Many plants stockpile this energy-storing polysaccharide in their roots instead of starch, and doctors still use it as the benchmark substance for testing kidney function — name the fiber?
Inulin are a group of naturally occurring polysaccharides produced by many types of plants, industrially most often extracted from chicory.
This Liverpool-born mathematician roamed from finite groups to knot theory, but is best loved for inventing a famous cellular automaton called the Game of Life — who was he?
John Horton Conway (26 December 1937 - 11 April 2020) was an English mathematician.
This fatal prion disease, once common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, was nicknamed 'laughing sickness' and spread through ritual funerary cannibalism. What is it?
Kuru (disease) was a rare, incurable, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was formerly common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea.
Born in 1880, this Australian therapist and part-time stage actor is remembered for coaching a stammering British monarch — who is he?
Lionel Logue (26 February 1880 - 12 April 1953) was an Australian speech and language therapist and amateur stage actor who helped King George VI manage his stammer.

An engineer and teacher from a poor family who once served as mayor of Tehran, this politician became Iran's sixth president in 2005 and was a fierce proponent of the country's nuclear program — who is he?
Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (n Sabbaghian; born 28 October 1956) is an Iranian politician who served as the sixth president of Iran from 2005 to 2013.
Driven by hormones, this coordinated pair of bodily rhythms — one governing the ovaries, the other the uterine lining — usually runs 21 to 35 days and begins around age 12. What is it called?
Menstrual cycle is a series of natural changes in hormone production and the structures of the uterus and ovaries of the female reproductive system that makes pregnancy possible.
A small terrestrial carnivore of the family Herpestidae that feasts mainly on insects, reptiles, and birds — and turns up as an introduced pest in Hawaii — what creature is it?
Mongoose is a small terrestrial carnivorous mammal belonging to the family Herpestidae.

Sometimes reaching two meters long but often thinner than a millimeter or two wide, these thread-like parasitoid worms turn up in damp puddles, troughs, and swimming pools as adults — what phylum is this?

Nematomorpha (sometimes called Gordiacea, and commonly known as horsehair worms, hairsnakes, or Gordian worms) are a phylum of parasitoid animals similar to yet distinct from nematode worms in morphology, hence the name.
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz, and named his improved early radio receiver the 'coherer' — whose key 'syntonic' tuning patents helped birth radio?
Oliver Lodge (12 June 1851 - 22 August 1940) was an English physicist and electrical engineer whose investigations into electromagnetic radiation (EMR) contributed to the development of radio.
This galliform game bird, native to Europe, Asia, and Africa, was once lumped in with pheasants and quail, but DNA suggests it isn't one distinct group at all — which bird is it?
Partridge is a medium-sized galliform bird in any of several genera, with a wide native distribution throughout parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.

Sitting at the intersection of textual criticism, literary criticism, history, and linguistics, this scholarly discipline studies language through oral and written historical sources — what is it called?
Philology (from Ancient Greek (philologa) 'love of word') is the study of language in oral and written historical sources.

This category of polymers, most commonly known in the form of PET, is prized for clothing but — unlike some of its naturally occurring plant and insect cousins — rarely biodegrades — what material is it?
Polyester is a category of polymers that contain one or two ester linkages in every repeat unit of their main chain.
Ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius believed this oratorical skill could profoundly move even those not present in the room — what is the term for addressing a live audience?
Public speaking is the delivery of a speech to a live audience.

Covering more than 100 conditions like lupus and Sjögren's syndrome and overlapping heavily with immunology, this branch of medicine tackles inflammation in the joints, muscles and bones — what is it called?

Rheumatology (from Ancient Greek (rhema) 'flowing current') is a branch of medicine devoted to the diagnosis and management of disorders of which the common feature is inflammation in the bones, muscles, joints, and internal organs.
This American painter turned inventor co-developed a telegraph system and became the namesake of the dot-dash code that helped make telegraphy commercially viable — who is he?
Samuel Morse (April 27, 1791 - April 2, 1872) was an American inventor and painter.
This macrofungus, native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, is now cultivated and consumed around the globe as one of its most widely eaten mushrooms. What mushroom is this?
Shiitake is a macrofungus native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, which is cultivated and consumed around the globe.

Native to China and Vietnam, this invasive planthopper species has spread destructively across the US, feasting on grapevines and stone fruit as well as its preferred invasive host tree — what insect is it?
Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is a species of planthopper indigenous to parts of China and Vietnam.

Caused by the spiral bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously announces itself with a single painless ulcer called a chancre, then a rash that loves the palms and soles — which sexually transmitted disease is it?

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum. The signs and symptoms depend on the stage it presents: primary, secondary, latent or tertiary.
What culinary herb — the dried aerial parts of plants in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean — is most commonly cultivated in its 'vulgaris' species from Southeast Europe?
Thyme is a culinary herb consisting of the dried aerial parts of some members of the genus Thymus of flowering plants in the mint family Lamiaceae.

This genus of giant theropod dinosaur, whose best-known species takes a Latin name meaning 'king,' roamed an island continent that is now western North America at the very end of the Cretaceous period — name the genus?

Tyrannosaurus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur. The type species Tyrannosaurus rex (rex meaning 'king' in Latin), often shortened to T. rex or colloquially T-Rex, is one of the best represented theropods.
This slender, short-legged predator's genus also includes polecats, stoats, and ferrets, and its smallest species is the tiniest carnivore on Earth — what animal is it?
Weasel are mammals of the genus Mustela of the family Mustelidae.
Discovered in 1807 and named for the Roman goddess of home and hearth, this is thought to be the second-largest asteroid and the only known rocky protoplanet still intact in the belt — which one?
4 Vesta: Second largest main-belt asteroid. Vesta (minor-planet designation: 4 Vesta) is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt, with a mean diameter of 525 kilometres (326 mi).
Native to sub-Saharan grasslands and woodlands, this animal is the largest living land species, with the largest recorded specimen standing nearly 13 feet tall at the shoulder — which species is it?
African bush elephant: Species of mammal. Its skin is grey with scanty hairs, and bending cracks which support thermoregulation by retaining water.

This exaggerated immune response occurs when the body mistakes a harmless substance for a threat, triggering histamine release from mast cells and conditions like hay fever or anaphylaxis. What is this reaction called?
Allergy: Immune system response to a substance that most people tolerate well.
This cosmopolitan family of water birds, found on every continent but Antarctica, groups together the ducks, geese, and swans — what is it?
Anatidae: Biological family of water birds. The family has a cosmopolitan distribution, occurring on all the world's continents except Antarctica.
Known by common names like greenfly and blackfly, these small sap-sucking insects reproduce via live-born nymphs without males, a trick called telescoping generations — what are they?
Aphid: Superfamily of insects. The group includes the fluffy white woolly aphids.
Originally conceived as the average Earth-Sun distance before its 2012 redefinition, this measure equals about 499 light-seconds and underpins the definition of the parsec — what is it called?
Astronomical unit: Mean distance between Earth and the Sun.
Sitting at the bottom of the forebrain and including the striatum and substantia nigra, this cluster of brain nuclei governs voluntary movement and habit formation — what is it called?
Basal ganglia: Group of subcortical nuclei involved in the motor and reward systems.
Also known as vitamin B7, this B vitamin is found in every living cell and is popularly sold as a supplement; isolated, it's a white needle-like crystal — what is it?
Biotin: Chemical compound and essential nutrient.
This rigid organ not only supports the body and enables movement but also manufactures both red and white blood cells and stores essential minerals — what is it?
Bone: Rigid organs of the skeleton of vertebrates.

Marketed as Wellbutrin, this atypical antidepressant doubles as a stop-smoking aid and stands out for not causing sexual dysfunction or weight gain — what is this norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor?
Bupropion: Medication mainly used for depression and smoking cessation.
Also known as Flinders rose, this perennial shrub with rounded fleshy leaves and white-to-pink flowers is native across circum-Mediterranean countries — what's the plant called?
Marketed as a COX-2 inhibitor, this NSAID treats arthritis pain and menstrual cramps but carries heart attack and stroke risk warnings — which drug?

Caused by a bacterium and often symptomless for weeks after exposure, this sexually transmitted infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility in women if untreated — which infection?
Chlamydia: Sexually transmitted bacterial infection. Chlamydia, or more specifically a chlamydia infection, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
Striking at the same hour every day for weeks at a time, usually around one eye, this excruciating neurological condition is considered one of the most painful known to medicine — what is it?
Cluster headache: Neurological disorder. The disease is considered among the most painful conditions known to medical science.

Native to Europe and North Africa, this member of the carrot family can grow to 8 feet tall, with hollow stems blotched dark maroon and a distinctly foul smell carried on the wind — which highly poisonous plant is this?
Conium maculatum: Poisonous plant. The plant is herbaceous, with no woody parts, and has a biennial lifecycle.
A creeping vine of the gourd family that originated across India, Nepal, and southern China, this plant comes in slicing, pickling, and seedless types — what is it?
Cucumber: Species of flowering plant with edible fruits.
Striking 48 to 72 hours after a heavy drinker's last drink, this potentially fatal condition brings hallucinations, seizures nicknamed 'rum fits,' and dangerously high body temperature — what is it?
Delirium tremens: Rapid onset of confusion caused by alcohol withdrawal.
Bred in Córdoba in the early 1900s to hunt wild boar and puma, this large mastiff-type breed's ancestry includes an extinct local fighting dog and a Bull Terrier — which breed is it?
Dogo Argentino: Argentine breed of dog. It was bred in the early twentieth century in Córdoba in central Argentina, primarily for hunting large game such as peccaries, wild boar, and pumas.
In 1990, this theoretical physicist became the first physicist ever awarded the Fields Medal, later becoming known as the practical founder of M-theory — who is he?
Edward Witten: American theoretical physicist. Witten is a researcher in string theory, quantum gravity, supersymmetric quantum field theories, and other areas of mathematical physics.
Serving as chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria, which ancient Greek polymath was the first known person to calculate Earth's circumference?
Eratosthenes: Greek librarian, mathematician, geographer, and poet.
Powerfully built with a small head, stocky body, and a coat of black, white, brown, and grey, this is the only species of its kind still living in the UK — what is it?
European badger: Species of mustelid. It is classified as least concern on the IUCN Red List due to its wide range and large, stable population size which is thought to be increasing in some regions.
When fibroblasts overproduce collagen after repeated injury or chronic inflammation, this permanent connective-tissue scarring can impair an organ's normal function — what is it called?
Fibrosis: Excess connective tissue in healing.
Native from the British Isles east to the Caucasus, this tree in the olive family is prized for wood that's flexible, strong, and lightweight — what is its scientific name?
Fraxinus excelsior: Species of deciduous tree.
Deriving its name from Greek words for 'earth' and 'study of', this branch of natural science examines rocks and the processes that have shaped the planet over time — what is it called?
Geology: Scientific study of Earth's physical composition.
This Intel co-founder proposed the famous observation that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every two years — who is he?
This inherited disorder leaves blood unable to clot properly, causing prolonged bleeding after injury and, in its two main forms, low levels of clotting factor VIII or IX — which condition?
Haemophilia: Genetic disease involving blood clotting.

Governed by rules laid out in a document called a blazon, this medieval discipline of coats of arms, crests, and mottoes may have arisen so knights could recognize commanders behind their helmets — what is it?
Heraldry: Discipline of the design and study of coats of arms.
Running from your shoulder to your elbow, this long arm bone has a constriction nicknamed the 'surgical neck' due to its tendency to fracture — which bone?
Humerus: Long bone of the upper arm. It connects the scapula and the two bones of the lower arm, the radius and ulna, and consists of three sections.
Named from an Ancient Greek word for 'intestinal obstruction,' this medical condition disrupts the gut's normal propulsive movement, whether from lost peristalsis or a physical blockage — what is it?
Ileus: Disruption to the propulsive ability of the intestine.
Native to Africa and Eurasia, this opportunistic canid can sustain a running pace of about 10 mph over long distances while hunting small mammals, birds, and reptiles — which animal?
A real estate magnate and Spanish–American War officer worth roughly $87 million, he was the richest passenger aboard the Titanic — and went down with it in 1912. Who was he?
John Jacob Astor IV: American businessman and Titanic passenger (1864–1912)
This classical physics model imagines matter as countless invisible particles in constant, random collisions, explaining pressure, temperature and viscosity alike — what is it?
Kinetic theory of gases: Understanding of gas properties in terms of molecular motion.

Caused by a bacterium that thrives in fresh water and can contaminate hot tubs and water tanks, this atypical pneumonia brings cough, high fever and muscle pains days after exposure — what's it called?
Legionnaires' disease: Form of atypical pneumonia. Legionnaires' disease is a form of atypical pneumonia caused by any species of Legionella bacteria, quite often Legionella pneumophila.

A domesticated South American camelid whose Quechua name the Spanish adopted, this herd animal can haul about a quarter of its body weight for miles and learns simple tasks after a few tries — what is it?
Llama: Species of wooly domesticated mammal.
Popular as companion birds despite conservation concerns for several species, these large, long-tailed, brightly colored New World parrots belong to the tribe Arini — what are they?
Macaw: Group of birds in the parrot family.
On April 3, 1973, this Motorola engineer made history's first public call from a handheld cell phone on a Manhattan sidewalk — who is he?

From a Greek word meaning 'change,' this term covers the enzyme-driven reactions that turn food into usable energy and building blocks while excreting waste — letting organisms grow and reproduce. What is it?
Metabolism: Set of chemical reactions in organisms.
Normally equal to 60 seconds, which unit of time has occasionally run 61 seconds long in UTC due to leap seconds, though a 59-second version has never actually occurred?
Minute: Unit of time equal to 60 seconds. The prime symbol ′ is also sometimes used informally to denote minutes.
Sold under the brand name Bactroban, this topical antibiotic treats impetigo and clears MRSA from the nose — what is it?
Derived from the Greek word for kidney, this medical specialty covers kidney function, disease, and treatments ranging from diet changes to dialysis and transplantation — which field?
Nephrology: Medical study concerned with the kidneys.
Built from a nitrogen-containing base, a five-carbon sugar, and a phosphate group, these molecules are the monomer building blocks of DNA and RNA — what are they called?
Nucleotide: Biological molecules constituting nucleic acids.
Nicknamed 'brittle bone disease,' this genetic disorder causes fragile bones and blue-tinted eye whites, usually stemming from faulty type I collagen — what is it?
Osteogenesis imperfecta: Group of genetic disorders resulting in fragile bones.

Native to southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina, this vine produces a round berry that turns yellow or dark purple at maturity, prized for its juicy, seed-filled interior — what is it, scientifically speaking?
Passiflora edulis: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.

Positioned behind the mouth and nasal cavity, this throat structure channels food toward the esophagus and air toward the larynx, with a flap of cartilage guarding against the two crossing paths — what is it?
Pharynx: Part of the throat that is behind the mouth and nasal cavity.

Derived in 1900 by a German physicist who proposed that an oscillator's energy could only change in discrete increments, this principle describes the spectral density of radiation from a black body at a given temperature — what is it called?
Planck's law: Spectral density of light emitted by a black body.
This common name describes small aquatic crustaceans with an exoskeleton and ten legs, especially popular in the UK and Commonwealth nations for larger swimming decapods — what is it?
Prawn: Common name applied to some types of crustaceans.
This seabird's large, colorful beak fades after breeding season, and its short wings beat up to 400 times a minute to keep it airborne — what bird is it?
Domesticated roughly 8,000 years ago, this Southeast Asian bird species is the primary wild ancestor of today's chickens — which bird?
Red junglefowl: Species of bird; ancestor of the chicken. The red junglefowl was the primary species to give rise to today's many breeds of chicken (G. g. domesticus).
Nicknamed the 'Bone,' this variable-sweep-wing heavy bomber was dreamed up to fuse the B-58's Mach 2 speed with the B-52's range and payload — which aircraft is it?
Rockwell B-1 Lancer: American strategic bomber.
Commonly known as elder, with its blossoms called elderflower and its fruit elderberry, this genus contains between 20 and 30 flowering plant species — which genus?
The sole living species in its genus, this coastal California evergreen is the tallest tree species on Earth, reaching over 116 meters and living 2,200 years or more. What is it?
Sequoia sempervirens: Species of tree. Sequoia sempervirens is the sole living species of the genus Sequoia in the cypress family Cupressaceae (formerly treated in Taxodiaceae).

Named in 1842 from Brazilian fossils and often called a saber-toothed tiger despite no close kinship to true tigers, this genus of prehistoric predator roamed the Americas until the early Holocene — which animal?
Smilodon: Extinct genus of saber-toothed cat.
With eight arms plus two extra tentacles for grabbing prey, this soft-bodied mollusc has an internal chitin rod called a gladius instead of a true skeleton — what creature is it?

A retired US Navy captain, this NASA astronaut became the first woman to fly on an orbital spacecraft's test flight in 2024 and had her ISS stay extended by more than nine months due to technical issues — who is she?
Sunita Williams: U.S. Navy officer and NASA astronaut (born 1965)
A math prodigy who abandoned academia in 1969 for a reclusive cabin life, the 'Unabomber' mailed bombs for 17 years and published a 35,000-word anti-technology manifesto — who was he?
Shaped like a butterfly and sitting in the neck just below the Adam's apple, this endocrine gland secretes hormones that regulate metabolic rate — which gland is it?
Thyroid: Endocrine gland in the neck. The lower two thirds of the lobes are connected by a thin band of tissue called the isthmus (pl.: isthmi).
This ester of glycerol and three fatty acids is the main constituent of body fat and a major component of human skin oils — what is it?
Triglyceride: Any ester of glycerol having all three hydroxyl groups esterified with fatty acids.
Before becoming the first woman in space aboard a solo 1963 flight that orbited Earth 48 times, this cosmonaut worked in a textile factory and skydove as a hobby — who is she?
Valentina Tereshkova: Russian cosmonaut and politician (born 1937)
Denoted by the Greek letter lambda, this measure of a repeating wave's spatial period shrinks as frequency rises for a wave moving at constant speed — what is it called?
Wavelength: Distance over which a wave's shape repeats.
Spread mainly by the oriental rat flea, this gram-negative bacterium caused the Black Death and the Plague of Justinian — what is it?
Yersinia pestis: Species of bacteria, cause of plague.
The symbol for caesium is Cs. Caesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cs and atomic number 55.
The symbol for livermorium is Lv. Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.

William Shatner (born March 22, 1931) is a Canadian actor.
In what year was Nina Dobrev born?

Burt Reynolds: Burton Leon Reynolds Jr. (February 11, 1936 – September 6, 2018) was an American actor.

In what year was David McCallum born?
David McCallum: David Keith McCallum (19 September 1933 – 25 September 2023) was a Scottish actor and musician.

Daniel Craig: Daniel Wroughton Craig ( CRAYG; born 2 March 1968) is an English actor.

Diane Kruger (German: [diˈaːnə ˈkʁuːɡɐ], née Heidkrüger; born 15 July 1976) is a German actress.
In what year was Steven Spielberg born?
Steven Spielberg: Steven Allan Spielberg (born December 18, 1946) is an American filmmaker.
In what year did Helen McCrory die?
Helen McCrory: Helen Elizabeth McCrory (17 August 1968 – 16 April 2021) was an English actress.

Moonfall is a 2022 science fiction disaster film co-written, directed, and produced by Roland Emmerich.
In what year was Dogtooth first released?
